title: The Seat I Nearly Kept
script: Narrator: [tired] The bus was crowded when I left work on Tuesday. I was tired, and I was happy to find the last empty seat near the door.
Narrator: At the next stop, an older man entered with two heavy bags. He held the rail, but the bus moved suddenly and he almost fell.
Narrator: I saw him, yet I waited for someone else to stand. For a few seconds, I told myself that my day had also been difficult.
Narrator: [regretfully] Then a schoolboy across from me started to rise. He was carrying a large backpack and looked more tired than I felt.
Narrator: I became ashamed. I stood first and offered my seat to the older man. He thanked me and placed his bags beside his feet.
Narrator: The boy smiled, and I smiled back. Nothing dramatic happened, but my mood changed at once.
Narrator: I understood that good manners often begin before anyone asks us for help. We have to notice people and act without waiting for praise.
Narrator: [reflective] The man later asked where I worked. We spoke quietly about the busy road and the rain that was coming.
Narrator: Before his stop, he thanked me again. I told him it was a small thing, and he said small things can make a hard journey easier.
Narrator: His words stayed with me. I had nearly chosen my own comfort while another person needed help.
Narrator: Now, when I enter a bus, I look around before I sit. If someone needs the seat more, the choice becomes simple.
Narrator: Respect is not only polite language. Sometimes it is a seat, a door held open, or a moment of attention.
Narrator: [warmly] That short ride taught me to notice people and help without waiting for praise.
